rounds.question: How should rerolls and banishes look and work in the part picker?
rounds.found: Rerolls and banishes share one stock: 3 at the start of a run, +1 for every overdrive. A reroll deals a new set of cards; a banish takes the chosen card out of the run for good and deals one in its place. Buttons: Y rerolls (like the retune knob), X banishes the card you're on. Also new: a key card is now a coin flip between a new key and a level-up, an overdrive brings one of each, and a new key shows up even when your key slots are full (you take one out, never the red key). Tell me in the notes if you'd rather call the stock something else.

options.title: Brass plates
options.note: Two brass plates under the cards, REROLL (Y) and BANISH (X), each showing your stock as lamps, beside the MELT THEM plate when it's open. Tap a plate on a phone. In each video: a reroll at 1 second (the cards wash with static light and new ones come up), then the second card is banished (BANISHED stamped across it as it drops away and a new card takes its place).

options.title: Tuning dial
options.note: A brass tuning dial at the lower right with your stock as lamps round its rim; Y (or a tap) spins it to reroll. A red BANISH tab hangs on the chosen card; X (or a tap on the tab) banishes it. In each video: a reroll at 1 second (the cards wash with static light and new ones come up), then the second card is banished (BANISHED stamped across it as it drops away and a new card takes its place).

options.title: Brass tokens
options.note: Your stock as brass tokens in the top right corner, one REROLL plate under the cards, and the red BANISH tab on the chosen card. In each video: a reroll at 1 second (the cards wash with static light and new ones come up), then the second card is banished (BANISHED stamped across it as it drops away and a new card takes its place).

rounds.question: How should the Blue Key's frost look on the glass?
rounds.found: The Blue Key (on trial, not in the picker yet): every word that misses it freezes a key beside it; a word through it pays x2, +1 per frozen key; a word that touches the ice without it breaks the ice. Frozen keys hold their place and letters above fall past them. In each 7-second video: four words freeze four keys (the red key and the green middle key sit next to the blue one, so you can see them frozen), then a word goes through the blue key and cashes in (the ice bursts, the blue key moves), two more keys freeze, then a word touches the ice without the blue key and the ice breaks.

options.title: Frost film
options.note: A pale icy film over each frozen key, with a little frost in two corners. The blue key itself: a cold blue letter, a blue glow, frost in its corners and a chip showing what it pays now (x2, +1 per frozen key). No outline, since the outline is the green key's.

options.title: Ice block
options.note: Each frozen key looks like a clear block of ice: a bright icy edge and a shine across it. The blue key itself: a cold blue letter, a blue glow, frost in its corners and a chip showing what it pays now (x2, +1 per frozen key). No outline, since the outline is the green key's.

options.title: Rime
options.note: No film: white frost grows in from all four corners of each frozen key, longer the longer it stays frozen. The blue key itself: a cold blue letter, a blue glow, frost in its corners and a chip showing what it pays now (x2, +1 per frozen key). No outline, since the outline is the green key's.

options.title: Blue letters
options.note: The frozen keys' letters turn icy blue, with one small frost mark. The quietest look. The blue key itself: a cold blue letter, a blue glow, frost in its corners and a chip showing what it pays now (x2, +1 per frozen key). No outline, since the outline is the green key's.

options.title: Frost web
options.note: A light icy film, plus moving frost lines joining each frozen key to the blue key, so the patch reads as one. The blue key itself: a cold blue letter, a blue glow, frost in its corners and a chip showing what it pays now (x2, +1 per frozen key). No outline, since the outline is the green key's.

rounds.question: How should the Green Key look on the glass?
rounds.found: The Green Key is the middle key: words through it add to its charge (the small green number), then score it. Each video: the key sits, gets charged (a word lands at about 1.5 s), then a word is traced through it. The second video of each shows it when the red key lands on the middle key too: both looks have to show and not get in each other's way.

options.title: Green ring
options.note: A glowing green frame around the middle key, like the red key's scan but as a ring outside the key. When the middle key is also the red key, both show.

options.title: Green letter
options.note: The middle key's letter itself glows green, with a soft green light behind it. When the middle key is also the red key, both show.

options.title: Charge level
options.note: Green light fills the key from the bottom up as its charge grows, like a level meter. When the middle key is also the red key, both show.

options.title: Magic eye
options.note: A little green tuning eye sits on the key's corner and opens wider as the charge grows. When the middle key is also the red key, both show.

options.title: Breathing
options.note: A soft green glow that breathes, faster and brighter the more charge it holds. When the middle key is also the red key, both show.

rounds.question: Where should the night's listener request show while you play?
rounds.found: The request is announced on the night intro plaque in every option (last picture). This is where it stays while you play. The example: A WORD WITH K, with LINK traced. Payout is still to be decided (see chat).

options.title: Lower plate
options.note: The request takes the lower brass plate (in place of NIGHT 4) in red stamping, with a small request lamp. When your traced word would fill it, the lamp and letters blink red and the plate glows.

options.title: On the dial
options.note: With nothing traced, the dial scrolls REQUEST: A WORD WITH K. While you trace, a red REQ blinks beside the word's value when it would fill it.

options.title: Pinned in the log
options.note: The request stays pinned as the log's top line in red ink, under a red line. When your word would fill it, the line lights up red.

options.title: Slip in the window
options.note: A paper slip tucked into the bottom of the window frame: REQUEST LINE, then the request in red. It glows when your word would fill it.

rounds.question: The caller and the card: right look?
rounds.found: PixelLab art: a silhouette in a fedora and trench coat (outside on the fire escape, behind the rain) and a cream index card. He slides in from the right, the card slides out under the sash, he slips away. The game stamps REQUEST and pencils the request on the card. It plays once at the start of each night, after the goal plaque. Pick 1 to keep it as is, or leave notes.

options.title: Caller drop-off
options.note: Videos on desk and phone, a close-up of the card, and the card glowing when your traced word (LINK) fills the request.

rounds.question: How should the red key stand out a bit more, keeping its look?
rounds.found: Every option keeps today's red scan line and adds one thing. The red key is the G in the second row. Each option opens on a 5-second video.

options.title: As now
options.note: The red scan line rolls down the key, with a soft red glow.

options.title: Breathing glow
options.note: The same key with a bigger, stronger red glow that slowly swells and fades.

options.title: Red frame
options.note: The key's frame glows red, pulsing gently.

options.title: Red field
options.note: The key's dark dots warm to a deep red behind the letter, so the whole key reads red.

options.title: Bright scan
options.note: A brighter, quicker scan line with a fading red trail behind it.

options.title: Red pulse
options.note: Every couple of seconds a red ring pulses out from the key and fades.

options.title: Glow + frame
options.note: Options 1 and 2 together.

rounds.question: How should the game show what each word still needs to bring?
rounds.found: Night 4 of the new curve (target 205), 70 in with 3 words left: 135 to go, 45 a word. 'Nearly there' is 185 in, 20 to go, 7 a word, with RAT (+10) traced so you see what keeping pace looks like. Pick one, or mix them.

options.title: As now
options.note: The top plate says what's left (135 TO GO); the night intro already says about how much a word.

options.title: Plate takes turns
options.note: The top plate switches every few seconds between 135 TO GO and 45 A WORD.

options.title: Mark on the tube
options.note: A brass mark sits on the tube where this word should reach to keep pace, with the cells up to it outlined. It lights when the traced word gets there.

options.title: Dial says the pace
options.note: The dial's number reads +10/45: what the word is worth over what a word needs. It only turns hot when the word keeps pace. With nothing traced, the dial scrolls NEED 45 A WORD.

options.title: Second plate
options.note: The lower plate says 45 A WORD instead of NIGHT 4 (the night stays on the dial's scroll and the night intro).

options.title: Plate turns + tube mark
options.note: Option 1 and option 2 together.

rounds.question: How should the top plate show your signal against the night's target?
rounds.found: Round 1: the mark on the tube is in. This round is only the top plate. Same night as before: night 4, target 205, 70 in ('Nearly there': 185 in). Every option also has the tube mark.

options.title: As now
options.note: 135 TO GO, stamped.

options.title: Stamped score / target
options.note: 70 / 205, stamped like the night plate.

options.title: Big score, small target
options.note: The score in the big bold lettering, / 205 small and lighter beside it.

options.title: Lit window
options.note: A dark window set into the plate, 70 / 205 lit in amber (the score brighter than the target).

options.title: Lit dots
options.note: The same window in the dial's dot lettering: 70 bright, /205 amber.

options.title: Both plates
options.note: 70 / 205 on the top plate and 135 TO GO on the lower one (the night number stays on the dial's scroll and the night intro).

rounds.question: Which lettering should the game use on its paper and brass (log, plates, sheets, menus)?
rounds.found: What the game uses now: our own 5x7 pixel 'ink' (log, labels, sheets), a bold doubled version 'key' (plates, titles: the 'big thick' one), lit dial dots (the dial, the night score, the run score drums), and two outside fonts only on the How to Play cards (Alfa Slab One titles, Special Elite text). Proposed rule: one lettering for everything printed on paper or brass, in two or three set sizes (small labels, figures, titles), and lit dots for anything that is a lit display. Each option shows the night report set in it (plates too). Pick one and it becomes the rule everywhere.

options.title: Small pixel ink (as now)
options.note: Our own 5x7 lettering, one small size for everything; values only stand out by color.

options.title: Our pixel ink, two sizes
options.note: The same thin lettering of ours, with figures half again as big. No new font, no thick type.

options.title: VT323
options.note: A thin, tall terminal font: reads like an old station readout. Free font, would be kept in the repo.

options.title: Pixelify Sans
options.note: A clean modern pixel font with a semibold for figures. Free font.

options.title: Silkscreen
options.note: Tiny square pixel capitals, very crisp, wide. Free font.

options.title: Special Elite
options.note: The typewriter face from the How to Play cards, for labels and figures alike (no slab).

rounds.question: Which screen finish ties the art together best?
rounds.found: Now as videos (Chris: the finishes have to be seen moving): each one shows a word sent and the night clearing, full screen and a close-up at true size. 1 and 2 cost almost nothing (cached pictures laid over each frame); 3, 4 and 5 use the haze, a shrunk copy of the whole frame each frame, so they cost more and would need checking on the Retroid.

options.title: None (as now)
options.note: No overlay, for comparison.

options.title: Lamp-lit room
options.note: A soft vignette darkens the screen's edges and a light warm tint pulls every piece toward the same lamplight. Two cached pictures a frame: about the cheapest option.

options.title: Film
options.note: The lamp-lit room plus a faint moving film grain over everything, so painted art, pixel art and lettering all share the same texture. Still cheap: four small noise tiles, reused.

options.title: Haze
options.note: A soft glow of the whole picture is laid back over it, so light spills a little past edges and the lit keys, lamps and window bloom into their surroundings. The most 'tied together' but costs the most: one shrunk copy of the frame each frame.

options.title: Soft tube screen
options.note: Fine scanlines, a little haze and a vignette: as if the whole room were on an old monitor. Brings back a light screen look we had dropped before.

options.title: All of it, light
options.note: Vignette, warm tint, faint grain, light haze and half-strength scanlines together, each turned down.

options.title: Moving tube screen
options.note: Chris's pick, made to move: scanlines that creep down, a soft light band that rolls slowly down the screen, a faint flicker, and the vignette. One baked picture plus a thin band each frame, about as cheap as option 1.

rounds.question: Where should the run score show while you play, and how should it count up?
rounds.found: Four ways to keep the run score on screen while playing, in the part picker, the melter and the upgrade (it hides on the night report and DEAD AIR, which show it big). In all four, when a word's beam lands in the tube its points fly up as a '+N' into the counter, which counts up with a climbing tick and flares. Each counter grows a place when the score needs it (never fewer than 5) and shrinks to fit its corner if a score gets huge. Each clip sends RAT (+5), then shows a big +248 word's worth landing so you can see a long count. Play opens the game in that style with RAT traced.

options.title: Rolling drums
options.note: A brass-framed mechanical counter in the bottom-left corner of the room. Each drum turns up to the next figure as the score counts, the frame flares when it lands. Unused places show dim zeros.

options.title: Glow tubes
options.note: A small wooden case of glass tubes, each figure burning orange. Any figure that changes flares white-hot, then settles. A new tube lights up when the score needs another place.

options.title: Big lit dot display
options.note: The night report's lit dot-matrix figures, smaller, in a dark brass-rimmed panel in the corner. Counts in white-hot, settles to amber, with commas.

options.title: On the bar's brass plate
options.note: No new box: the lower brass plate in the bar shows the run score instead of the night number (the night is still announced at the start of each night and on the report). The plate glows and the figures pop while it counts.

rounds.question: How should the Gold Key look and behave on the glass?
rounds.found: Five new looks plus the one in the game now. Every clip is the same moves: the gold key at rest, L-I-N traced, then the gold key (it becomes the E of LINE), the word sent; then the same again with the gold key also being the red key. In the five new looks the key shows the letter it stands for once the word is real, and that letter flies to the tower in gold (today it stays a "?"). All of them cost the same as the current look on Retroid-size screens (within measuring noise). Play opens with the Gold Key fitted; put "goldred" in place of "gold" in the link to try it as the red key.

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: a gold "?" with a soft gold glow. It stays a "?" while traced and flies to the tower as an ordinary amber "?". As the red key too, it's the gold "?" with the red scan line over it.

images.label: Clip: a word through it, then as the red key too
Close-up: at rest and in a word (top), the same as the red key (bottom)

options.title: Letter reel
options.note: Letters roll slowly up through the key like a reel, with two small gold pointers at its sides, so it reads as "any letter". Trace it and the reel spins fast; the moment your word is real the right letter rolls up from below and locks with a white flash and a ring of light. That letter lifts off and flies to the tower in gold, and the tower light flashes gold. As the red key: the same reel on a dark red field with the red scan line and a red glow beside the gold.

images.label: Clip: a word through it, then as the red key too
Close-up: at rest and in a word (top), the same as the red key (bottom)

options.title: Gold lamp board
options.note: The whole key is softly lit gold with a bright "?"; a slow shimmer crosses it and small star glints come and go. When your word is real the "?" melts into the letter and glints fly off the key. Sent in gold with a gold flash on the tower. As the red key: the board runs from gold at the top to red embers at the bottom, with the red scan line.

images.label: Clip: a word through it, then as the red key too
Close-up: at rest and in a word (top), the same as the red key (bottom)

options.title: Shows its letter
options.note: The calmest look, and the one that helps you play: a breathing gold "?". When the letters you've traced could finish on the gold key, it shows the letter it would be (it comes and goes with the "?") before you pick it, and its edge glows brighter. Picked, it becomes that letter with a quick flash. Sent in gold. As the red key: gold letter on a dark red field with the red scan line.

images.label: Clip: a word through it, then as the red key too
Close-up: at rest and in a word (top), the same as the red key (bottom)

options.title: Brass housing
options.note: The gold key gets its own housing: a brass bezel with four rivets round a small dark window, and a sheen that slides along the brass now and then. Traced, the brass lights up. When the word is real the "?" closes to a bright line and the letter opens out of it, like a flap turning over. Sent in gold, and the signal comes down from the tower into the tube in gold too. As the red key: the window glows red behind the gold letter, with the red scan line.

images.label: Clip: a word through it, then as the red key too
Close-up: at rest and in a word (top), the same as the red key (bottom)

options.title: Gilded word
options.note: The gold spreads: a gold "?" sends out a slow ring of light at rest, and when your word is real every key in the word turns gold (letters, edges, arrows) with a ring opening from each. The whole word flies to the tower in gold, the tower flashes gold and the signal lands in the tube in gold. As the red key: the word is gold and the red scan line runs through every key of it.

images.label: Clip: a word through it, then as the red key too
Close-up: at rest and in a word (top), the same as the red key (bottom)

rounds.question: How should the label on each part case look (NEW, STACKS X2, SWAP A PART, RARE: ONCE ONLY)?
rounds.found: The label used to sit over the case's bottom border and long ones ran off. Four ways to fix it. Each picture shows an overdrive picker with all four kinds of label: a part you already have (stacks), the rare Gold Key, and parts that need a swap (phone and Retroid) or are new (computer).

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: a dark chip low in the case that sits over its bottom border, and long labels run off it.

options.title: Brass tab
options.note: A small brass plate stamped with the label, sitting inside the case above its bottom border, like the name plate above it. Rare parts get a gold-tinted tab.

options.title: Dial window
options.note: A little dark lit window with the label in the radio's amber dot lights; rare parts get a gold rim and gold dots.

options.title: Lit line
options.note: No box at all: a thin brass rule near the foot of the case with the label lit underneath. The cleanest; rare parts get a gold rule.

options.title: Top badge
options.note: A rounded badge riding the top edge of the case, over its frame, so it's the first thing you see. Rare parts get a gold badge.

rounds.question: What should fill the dark strips beside the logo in the title glass?
rounds.found: Your painted logo is the old 4x4 shape and the radio's glass is now the wider 5x5 shape, so there's a strip each side. Five ways to deal with it, none of them stretch the painting. Pictures on a computer, a phone and the Retroid's screen; play opens the title with that option.

options.title: As now
options.note: For comparison: your painted glass at its true shape, with a dark strip down each side of the wider 5x5 glass.

options.title: Blank keys
options.note: The painting's own blank corner keys carry on out to the frame on both sides, lined up with each row, so the grid just looks wider. Nothing is stretched; the logo stays exactly as painted.

options.title: Soft edges
options.note: The strips stay, but they glow faintly and the painting's edges melt into them, so there's no hard black bar. The smallest change.

options.title: Thicker frame
options.note: The radio's own wood from just outside the glass is copied inside at its true size, so the opening fits the picture: the frame looks a little heavier.

options.title: Band scales
options.note: A lit tuning scale fills each strip, like the station markings on an old radio: kilocycles down the left, megacycles down the right.

options.title: Zoom to fill
options.note: The picture is enlarged to fill the glass. No strips, but the tops of LEXI and the bottom of AL get cut. Shown so you can see why I'd avoid it.

rounds.question: Which take on the dot glass letters do you like best?
rounds.found: Six takes on the look the game has now, each with one idea, plus today's look for comparison. Every video is the same ten seconds: RAT is traced and becomes a word, it is sent and reaches the tower, new keys fall in, four letters are picked and taken back. The play links open the game with RAT traced in that look. All of them draw as fast as today's look or a little faster (measured at 640x480 on a slowed-down processor). Ideas can be combined: say which ones you want together. Chris picked deep glass with the clear path arrows and the lift-off together; that is now the game's look.

options.title: Dot glass (now)
options.note: The game as it is today, for comparison: flat dark keys, the line through the letters, the light wipe over a real word, letters breaking into dots when sent, keys scrambling as they land.

options.title: Deep glass
options.note: Richer glass. Every key sits in a recessed well (dark under its top lip, the lower lip catching the light), each letter throws a soft glow on the dots round it, and the pane gets a faint curved reflection, darker corners and a glint that slides across now and then. Plays exactly the same.

options.title: Warm-up
options.note: Keys power on as they arrive. A falling key rides dark; when it seats, its whole letter strikes on with a short stutter (dark, a white flash, dim, then settling to amber) instead of the scramble of dots. The start of a night and every refill look like the set warming up.

options.title: Word lock
options.note: A stronger real-word moment. When the letters become a word every key of it flashes together, a ring of light opens out from each, the keys get a thick pale-gold frame and breathe as one, and the rest of the glass dips so the word stands alone. Replaces the light wipe.

options.title: Clear path
options.note: The traced order without anything crossing a letter. Lit links run from the edge of one key to the edge of the next and end in an arrowhead, a bead runs along each link, and a lit stud marks the first key. Replaces the line through the middles and the ring.

options.title: Lift-off
options.note: A more satisfying send. The letters rise whole off the glass, bigger and brighter, while the fill drains away down the keys under them and an ember of each letter fades; then they come apart into dots from up there, with a few sparks, and stream to the tower. The send takes about a tenth of a second longer.

options.title: Side meter
options.note: Deeper, more orange amber, and the value moved out of the letter's dot field: a stack of four small lamp sockets in the right edge of each key, one lit per value step, so the letter stands alone and the value reads like a little level meter.

rounds.question: How should the title menu look under the radio?
rounds.found: Five ways, four of them with each option in its own container on dark floorboards (no bare black). Pictures for a computer and a phone; play links open the title with that look (left/right or up/down to choose, A to pick).

options.title: Bar and parchment (now)
options.note: What you didn't like, for comparison: the game's wood-and-brass bar across the bottom with one parchment holding the list.

options.title: Brass plates
options.note: Dark floorboards under the sideboard, each option on its own brass plate side by side. The chosen one is lit from behind with a red arrow; the other sits in shadow.

options.title: Station buttons
options.note: Each option is a big cream push button, like the preset keys on an old radio. The chosen one is pressed in and glows amber.

options.title: Dial windows
options.note: Each option is its own little lit display in a brass rim, lettered in the radio's dot-matrix lights. The chosen one burns bright; the other is dim.

options.title: Parchment tags
options.note: Each option is a parchment tag hanging from the radio's base on brass chains. The chosen one is lit and sways gently.

rounds.question: How should the Carrier Lamp's red key look?
rounds.found: Five ways to mark the red key (it doubles any word that uses it), all without the red outline. Each clip shows the key on its own, then picked into a word: every look keeps it red when picked. Play links open the game with the Carrier Lamp fitted.

options.title: Red letter
options.note: The key's letter is lit red instead of amber, with a soft red glow round it. Picked, it fills red.

options.title: Red backlight
options.note: The letter stays amber; the dots behind it glow a dim, breathing red, like a red bulb behind the panel.

options.title: Ember fill
options.note: A low red glow sits in the bottom of the key and gently rises and falls, like embers.

options.title: Pilot lamp
options.note: A small red pilot lamp in the key's corner, softly pulsing, and its value dots turn red. The quietest of the five.

options.title: Red scan
options.note: A red line keeps sweeping down the key, like a signal being picked up.

rounds.question: Which title screen should the game open on?
rounds.found: Six ways in. The bar is now away on the title screen and rises into place with a clunk when you start. Options 1-5 use a placeholder logo made from the game's own letters (the real one drops into the same spot later); 6 spells the title in the radio's keys. Watch the clips, or play each one: press A once to skip the entrance, again to start. You can mix pieces.

options.title: Tuning in
options.note: The room starts dark with static and the dial hunting. Scrambled letters flicker and lock into the logo left to right, it lands with a thump, then the six lamps come on one by one.

options.title: From the tower
options.note: Rings of red signal leave the tower's beacon and wash across the room. The logo forms out of wavy lines that settle into the letters, then it burns in.

options.title: Neon across the street
options.note: The logo is a neon sign on a dark board. The letters buzz on one at a time, stutter, and flood the room red; SIGNAL lights up in amber under it.

options.title: Fill the tube
options.note: The signal tube along the bar fills itself cell by cell. When it's full the room flashes and the logo drops in on a brass plate with a heavy clunk and a bounce.

options.title: Programme sheet
options.note: Parchment, like the old title box: a sheet slides up, the logo is stamped onto it, SIGNAL comes up in red ink and the two lines of how to play type out.

options.title: Radio close-up
options.note: Your sketch, with your painted glass. No bar, the radio big and centred (a clean 1.5x). Static in the glass, then each letter of your picture switches on in reading order with a stutter and a blip; once lit they breathe, and now and then one flickers out for a moment. The dial scrolls, the meter swings up, the lamps come on and a brass PRESS START plate appears.

rounds.question: Which look should the letter keys in the radio glass have?
rounds.found: Six looks for the play area, all in the same room with the same value dots and the same lit state for traced keys. Play any of them in the game (press Select/Tab in the game to flip between all six too). Pick one, or tell me what to mix.

options.title: Pixel keys
options.note: Chunky pixel letters on dark keys; traced keys light up amber with dark letters. Matches the room's pixels exactly.

options.title: Typewriter
options.note: Round cream caps in brass rings with typed ink letters; traced keys glow warm.

options.title: Glow tubes
options.note: Dark glass with a fine mesh and thin orange letters burning inside, like old display tubes.

options.title: Neon glass
options.note: No keys at all: glowing letters floating in the smoked glass, traced ones burn white.

options.title: Ivory tiles
options.note: Chunky ivory game tiles with engraved letters; traced tiles turn gold.

options.title: Brass keys
options.note: Polished brass plates with stamped letters; traced plates flare bright.

rounds.question: Which play-area direction should we build on?
rounds.found: Five whole treatments of the glass, not just letter styles: how keys rest, light up, link together, lock when the word is good, leave for the tower and land. All stay dark with smooth warm glow and keep the value dots. In every one the glass flares when a word leaves, catches a red glint when the beacon answers, and its rim pulses red on your last word. Watch the clip, then play it. Pick one, or tell me which pieces to combine.

options.title: Valve bank
options.note: Your glow tubes taken all the way. Every key is a little valve: the letter is a hot filament that flutters, flares when the key lands and fills its glass with haze when traced. A live wire with current running down it joins the letters, and a sent letter leaves its valve dark for a moment.

options.title: Signal scope
options.note: No keys at all: the glass is one instrument screen. Green letters on a fine grid; the trace is a live wave that wanders while you search, then stands clean and turns gold when the word locks. Rings close in on traced letters and falling letters leave an afterglow.

options.title: Stencil plates
options.note: Heavy dark iron plates with the letters cut through them, and the radio's valves burning behind. You read the letters by the light in the cuts. Sent plates leave holes you can see the valves through, until the next plates slam down and shut the light off. Value dots are small drilled holes.

options.title: Switchboard
options.note: Every key is a jewel lamp in a brass ring. Tracing plugs a braided cord from lamp to lamp (it swings, then settles) and the lamp lights up. When the word locks the cords pull tight and a chase runs down the lamps; when you send, the cords drop away.

options.title: Dot glass
options.note: The keys are small lamp boards, cousins of the dial. A traced board fills up from the bottom and its letter goes white. A sent word comes apart into its dots, which stream out to the tower. Boards scramble for a blink when they land.

rounds.question: How should a gold, one-time part look different from the regular parts, on its picker card and in its slot?
rounds.found: Chris wants more one-time gold parts, and the gold key's card and slot barely look different from the others now. Each option shows the picker (the Gold Key is the middle card) and the bar with the Gold Key fitted in the third slot. The cards' label also changes from RARE: ONCE ONLY to GOLD PART: ONE ONLY. All are drawn once and cached, except the glint, which only draws while it sweeps.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: A thin yellow line round the card and a soft glow; the slot looks like any other.

options.title: Gilded
options.note: The case frame, its name plate and the part's slot frame are recolored from brass to bright gold, pixel by pixel (the art's own shading kept), with a soft gold glow behind the slot.

options.title: Gilded + glint
options.note: Gilded, and every few seconds a band of light sweeps along the gold frame of the card and the slot. Watch the videos.

options.title: Jewel box
options.note: Gilded, with a crimson velvet lining inside the case and the slot, like a jewelry box. Reads as special even at a glance on the bar.

options.title: Gold seal
options.note: The case and slot stay brass, but a round gold medallion with an engraved star sits on their top-right corner: a stamp that says this one is different.

options.title: All in
options.note: Gilded + glint + the gold seal together.

rounds.question: Which music should play under the game while you spell (the main play screen)?
rounds.found: Chris wants chill 1930s-40s jazz, low and smooth, like a band playing in the next room. All four are made by the game itself as it runs (synthesized, no recordings, so the game stays small and the music never repeats exactly), heard through a wall: the highs rolled off and a little room echo, with the room's rain under it, turned down to about a third of its old level (Chris found it too loud over the music; the game's rain gets the same cut when the music goes in). Each clip is 75 seconds. They're turned up here so you can hear them; in the game they'd sit low under the rain. Pick one (or mix: say what you like from each) and I'll tune it in a second round. Decided 2026-11-14: none of them. Chris keeps the game's own music, since its tones match the game's sounds; the rain was turned down instead.

options.title: Piano trio, late ballad
options.note: Piano, brushes and an upright bass at 70 BPM, a slow minor tune with the piano taking the melody now and then.

options.title: Small band with a muted horn
options.note: A gentle swing at 96 BPM: walking bass, brushes and ride, piano chords, and a cup-muted trumpet playing short phrases every few bars.

options.title: Old 78 record through the wall
options.note: 84 BPM (your tempo): the band with a clarinet, as an old record would sound from the next room: narrow, warm, crackling, the pitch wavering slightly.

options.title: Vibraphone after hours
options.note: Very slow (62 BPM) and dreamy: a vibraphone with its tremolo over soft bass, the lightest brushes, a few piano chords.

rounds.question: How should each night start, so it's clear how much signal you need?
rounds.found: Chris: not enough clarity on how many points each night needs; a night intro you press past. Options 1-4 hold until you press A (or tap); the bar's top plate keeps showing what's left once you're playing. Every option shows the same facts: the night, the signal to beam, your words and retunes (parts that add to them are counted in), and the average a word needs. Shown on night 3 with a Spare Battery fitted. 'Play in game' opens that night with the card up.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: The brass plaque drops in at the top, holds about three seconds and lifts away by itself; any press sends it off sooner.

options.title: Big brass plaque
options.note: A large brass plaque over the dimmed room: NIGHT 3, the signal to beam in big red stamped figures, the words and retunes you have, and about how much each word needs to average. It waits for A.

options.title: Night ledger
options.note: A parchment card like the log: the night's terms on ruled lines (signal to beam, words, retunes, about a word), with what your parts add noted on their line. It waits for A.

options.title: On the radio's glass
options.note: The letters go dark and the glass itself lights up with the goal in the dial's dot lettering, the big number in the middle; the room stays lit. It waits for A.

options.title: Full-screen title card
options.note: The whole screen goes dark like an old film's title card: NIGHT THREE, a red beacon dot, the target big in cream, then you have 7 words and 1 retune, about 19 a word. It waits for A.

rounds.question: How should the bar and the run score stand out from the room, without making the room darker?
rounds.found: Chris: make our interface stand out over the background a bit more without darkening it or breaking anything. Each option is cheap (a few fills a frame, or one grayed copy of the room made once). 'Close up' shows the run score and the bar's top edge; 'Play in game' opens a word in progress with that option.

options.title: As it is now
options.note: The bar and the run score sit straight on the room, lit like the room.

options.title: Cast shadow
options.note: A soft shadow falls on the room just above the bar and under the run score, as if they stand in front of the wall.

options.title: Rim of lamplight
options.note: A warm line of light along the bar's top edge and the run score's top, as if the lamp catches their brass.

options.title: Dark keyline
options.note: A thin dark line round the run score and along the top of the bar, separating them from the room like a printed outline.

options.title: Room less colorful
options.note: The room (wallpaper, radio, sideboard, window) a little grayer at the same brightness, so the warm brass and parchment read stronger. Made once, costs nothing per frame.

options.title: Shadow and rim
options.note: Options 1 and 2 together.
